steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Perception is the process of interpreting sensory information to make sense of the world. Sensation is detecting stimuli; perception is interpreting them - they are distinct processes.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Gregory's constructivist theory: perception uses past experience and expectations to interpret sensory input (top-down processing). Visual illusions support this - we misinterpret because we apply assumptions (e.g. the Muller-Lyer illusion).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Gibson's direct theory: perception is entirely determined by sensory input from the environment (bottom-up processing). We perceive affordances - what the environment offers us (e.g. a chair affords sitting). No past experience needed.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Factors affecting perception: culture (Hudson's study showed Western and non-Western people perceive depth cues differently), emotion (anxious people perceive threats more readily), motivation (hungry people are more likely to perceive food-related images).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Compare Gregory's constructivist theory with Gibson's direct theory of perception. | Explain how culture can affect perception, using research evidence. | Evaluate what visual illusions tell us about the nature of perception.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Sensation = detecting. Perception = interpreting. They are different processes. Gregory = top-down (experience-based). Gibson = bottom-up (environment-based). Always name a SPECIFIC illusion (Muller-Lyer, Ames Room) when discussing perception.
